ladders.title: Power required: derive, plot, then altitude, turns and winglets
ladders.freq: Named signature ask of the aircraft design chair: power required derived and plotted, with altitude, turns and winglets
ladders.figure: Blank axes of power P up the side and true airspeed V along the bottom, labelled level flight at sea level with W, S, C_D0 and K given, and the request to derive P_R(V) and plot it.

rungs.ask: Level flight. Write power required as a function of speed.
rungs.answer: P_R = DV with D = qSC_D0 + KW²/(qS), so P_R = ½ρV³SC_D0 + 2KW²/(ρVS). The parasite term grows as V³ and the induced term falls as 1/V.
rungs.say: Power required is drag times speed, with a parasite term in V³ and an induced term in 1/V

rungs.ask: Plot it and mark the special speeds.
rungs.answer: A bucket. Minimum power sits at C_L = √(3C_D0/K), where induced drag is three times parasite drag. The ray from the origin touches the curve at minimum drag, C_L = √(C_D0/K), at 3^(1/4) ≈ 1.32 times the minimum power speed.
rungs.say: The bottom of the bucket is minimum power, and the tangent ray from the origin marks minimum drag

rungs.ask: Why does the tangent from the origin give minimum drag?
rungs.answer: P_R/V = D, so the slope of a ray from the origin to a point on the curve is the drag there; the shallowest ray that still touches the curve is minimum drag, the (L/D)max point.
rungs.say: The slope of a ray from the origin is P/V, which is drag

rungs.ask: Add power available for a jet and for a prop. Where is the best climb rate?
rungs.answer: Jet thrust is roughly constant, so P_A = TV is a ray through the origin. Prop power P_A = η_pP_shaft is roughly flat. RC_max = (P_A − P_R)_max/W at the largest vertical gap: near minimum power speed for the prop, at a higher speed for the jet. Top speed is the right-hand crossing.
rungs.say: Rate of climb is excess power over weight, read at the largest vertical gap

rungs.ask: Now climb to altitude. What happens to the curve?
rungs.answer: At the same W and C_L, V scales by √(ρ₀/ρ) and so does P_R = WV/(L/D), so every point slides out along a ray through the origin by √(ρ₀/ρ). Power available falls with density, the gap closes, and the curves touch at the absolute ceiling.
rungs.say: At the same lift coefficient, speed and power both scale by √(ρ₀/ρ), so the curve slides out along rays from the origin

rungs.ask: Hold a level turn at load factor n.
rungs.answer: Lift becomes nW, so only the induced term changes: P_R = ½ρV³SC_D0 + 2Kn²W²/(ρVS). The low speed side rises by n², the minimum power point moves to higher speed, and stall speed rises by √n.
rungs.say: In the turn lift is nW, so the induced term picks up n²

rungs.ask: Add winglets. What moves?
rungs.answer: Winglets raise span efficiency e, which lowers K = 1/(πeAR). The induced term shrinks, so the low speed side drops most and the minimum power and minimum drag speeds move lower. The added wetted area raises C_D0 slightly, lifting the high speed end a little.
rungs.say: Winglets lower K, which mostly lowers the induced, low speed side of the curve

rungs.ask: So when are winglets worth it?
rungs.answer: When induced drag is a large share of the total: heavy, slow, high C_L flight such as climb and long range cruise at high weight. Extra span gives a larger gain, so winglets pay where a gate, hangar or wing structure caps the span.
rungs.say: Winglets pay off where induced drag dominates and span is capped

rungs.ask: Now take the same airplane to Mars.
rungs.answer: ρ ≈ 0.020 kg/m³ and g = 3.71 m/s², so W falls to 0.38 of Earth's. At the same C_L, V scales as √(W/ρ), about 4.8 times the Earth speed, and P_R = WV/(L/D) is about 1.8 times. The bucket moves far right and up, which drives big wings, low wing loading and high C_L flight.
rungs.say: Speed scales as √(W/ρ) at fixed C_L, so the Mars curve moves to about 4.8 times the speed and 1.8 times the power

ladders.trap: Write P_R = ½ρV³SC_D0 + 2KW²/(ρVS), then move it along rays through the origin with altitude, put n² on the induced term in a turn, and lower K for winglets.

ladders.title: Carrier aircraft: wind over deck, catapult and W versus V plots
ladders.freq: Carrier operations (wind over deck, W versus V plots, catapult) is a named aircraft design chair ask, and carrier sizing appeared on a recent real board
ladders.figure: Side view of a carrier deck with an aircraft at the start of the catapult stroke, the ship moving into a headwind, and blank axes of weight W against speed V.

rungs.ask: What is wind over deck, and why does it matter?
rungs.answer: Wind over deck V_WOD is the relative wind along the deck: ship speed plus the natural headwind component. Wings need airspeed, so the catapult only supplies end speed V_end = V_launch − V_WOD, and on landing the engaging speed relative to the deck is V_approach − V_WOD.
rungs.say: The airplane cares about airspeed, and the ship supplies part of it as wind over deck

rungs.ask: What sets the minimum launch airspeed?
rungs.answer: A margin above stall in the launch configuration, typically 1.1 V_stall with V_stall = √(2W/(ρSC_Lmax)), plus enough excess thrust to accelerate and climb away after the bow.
rungs.say: Launch airspeed is a margin above stall, about 1.1 V_stall, with excess thrust to climb away

rungs.ask: Draw the launch W versus V plot.
rungs.answer: Required launch airspeed grows as √W, so W ∝ V² rises across the plot. Catapult energy E_max limits ½(W/g)V_end² ≤ E_max, so available end speed √(2gE_max/W) falls as W rises. Add V_WOD to the capability curve; the crossing gives the maximum launch weight.
rungs.say: Required airspeed grows with √W while catapult end speed falls with weight, and the crossing sets maximum launch weight

rungs.ask: Now the catapult itself. How hard does it push?
rungs.answer: V_end² = 2as, so a = V_end²/(2s). A 90 m stroke to 70 m/s needs about 27 m/s², about 2.8 g mean, which sets the nose gear tow loads and airframe launch loads.
rungs.say: End speed squared equals twice the acceleration times the stroke

rungs.ask: Landing. What sets the approach speed, and why is it so strict?
rungs.answer: Approach at about 1.15 V_stall in the power approach configuration. The arresting gear absorbs ½(W/g)(V_approach − V_WOD)², so its energy limit caps landing weight, and a low approach speed demands high C_Lmax and low wing loading.
rungs.say: Approach speed is a margin above stall, and the arresting gear absorbs the engaging kinetic energy

rungs.ask: Draw the landing W versus V plot.
rungs.answer: Approach airspeed rises as √W. Arresting gear capability gives a maximum engaging speed that falls with weight. Wind over deck lowers the needed engaging speed. The crossing gives the maximum trap weight, which sets the bring-back weight of fuel and stores.
rungs.say: The crossing of approach speed and arresting gear capability sets the bring-back weight

rungs.ask: How does this show up on the constraint diagram?
rungs.answer: Launch and approach each give a vertical wing loading line, W_TO/S ≤ ½ρV_stall²C_Lmax/β, each at its own weight fraction β and its own V_stall from the required speed margin. Carrier designs therefore sit at lower W/S than land-based fighters, and the wave-off climb gives a thrust line.
rungs.say: Launch and approach become vertical wing loading lines at their own weight fractions

rungs.ask: Take the catapult away. Launch from a ski jump.
rungs.answer: The ramp gives an upward flight path angle and vertical velocity, which buys time to accelerate to flying speed along a ballistic arc. Launch then depends on T/W and deck run, so ski jump designs carry high thrust loading and a lower launch weight.
rungs.say: The ski jump trades catapult energy for time in the air to accelerate along a ballistic arc

ladders.trap: Work in airspeed: catapult end speed plus wind over deck reaches about 1.1 V_stall, and energy limits ½(W/g)V² give the falling capability curves on the W versus V plots.

ladders.title: From circulation to induced drag, elliptic loading and winglets
ladders.freq: Aerodynamics in 5 of 11 terms and 6 aircraft design chair sessions; circulation, L' = ρVΓ and root bending moment are on the classic slips list
ladders.figure: Top view of a straight wing of span b in a freestream V∞ with trailing vortex lines drawn behind it, and above it blank axes of circulation Γ against spanwise position y from −b/2 to b/2.

rungs.ask: Connect lift to circulation.
rungs.answer: Kutta-Joukowski: lift per unit span L' = ρVΓ. The Kutta condition at the sharp trailing edge fixes Γ for each section.
rungs.say: Lift per unit span is ρVΓ, the Kutta-Joukowski theorem

rungs.ask: Sketch Γ(y). What happens at the tips, and what does the wing leave behind?
rungs.answer: Pressure equalizes at the tips, so Γ falls to zero there. A vortex filament keeps its strength along its length (Helmholtz), so every change dΓ/dy sheds trailing vorticity of strength −(dΓ/dy)dy, which rolls up into the tip vortices.
rungs.say: Every change in circulation along the span sheds a trailing vortex

rungs.ask: Find the downwash at the wing.
rungs.answer: Biot-Savart on the semi-infinite trailing sheet: w(y₀) = −(1/(4π))∫_{−b/2}^{b/2} (dΓ/dy)/(y₀ − y) dy, with w positive upward, so lift gives a downward w. At the wing it is half the far wake value.
rungs.say: I apply Biot-Savart to the semi-infinite trailing vortex sheet

rungs.ask: Where does induced drag come from?
rungs.answer: Downwash tilts the local relative wind by α_i = −w/V. The local lift ρVΓ is perpendicular to that local wind, so it tilts back by α_i and gives D'_i = L'α_i. Integrated: D_i = ∫ L'α_i dy, the energy carried away in the wake.
rungs.say: The downwash tilts the local lift vector back, and the backward component is induced drag

rungs.ask: Which distribution minimizes induced drag for given lift and span?
rungs.answer: Elliptic: Γ = Γ₀√(1 − (2y/b)²). Downwash is constant, w = −Γ₀/(2b), α_i = C_L/(πAR), so C_Di = C_L²/(πAR) with e = 1.
rungs.say: Elliptic loading gives uniform downwash and the minimum induced drag for given lift and span

rungs.ask: Now a general distribution. Give me e.
rungs.answer: With y = −(b/2)cos θ, Γ = 2bV Σ A_n sin nθ. C_L = πAR A₁ and C_Di = C_L²(1 + δ)/(πAR) with δ = Σ_{n≥2} n(A_n/A₁)², so e = 1/(1 + δ) ≤ 1.
rungs.say: Lift comes from A₁ alone, and every higher term adds induced drag

rungs.ask: How do you get elliptic loading on a real wing?
rungs.answer: An elliptic planform with zero twist, or a tapered planform with taper ratio near 0.4 plus twist. Planform and twist both shape Γ, and twist tunes the loading for one design C_L.
rungs.say: Planform and twist together shape the loading, and twist sets it for one design C_L

rungs.ask: Now add winglets. How do they help?
rungs.answer: At fixed projected span, a vertical extension spreads the trailing vorticity over a taller wake, so this nonplanar system reaches e above 1 based on projected span. Adding the same length as span gives a larger gain, so winglets pay where span is capped; they also add wetted area and some root bending moment.
rungs.say: Winglets spread the wake vertically, which raises e for a fixed projected span

rungs.ask: Fix root bending moment instead of span. What is the best loading now?
rungs.answer: With lift and root bending moment fixed and span free, the optimum takes a longer span with load shifted inboard, a bell-shaped distribution, and lower induced drag than the elliptic wing of the original span.
rungs.say: With bending moment fixed, the optimum is a longer span with a bell-shaped, inboard-heavy loading

ladders.trap: State L' = ρVΓ, shed trailing vorticity from every dΓ/dy, and use α_i = C_L/(πAR) for elliptic loading so C_Di = C_L²/(πeAR) with e = 1 at the planar optimum.

ladders.title: Drag polar to range and endurance, jet and prop, then a new planet
ladders.freq: Performance and drag polar themes recur across aircraft design chair sessions; range on a real recent board reduced to drag minimization
ladders.figure: Blank axes of C_L against C_D with the parabolic polar C_D = C_D0 + KC_L² written beside them, and two engine labels: jet with fuel flow c_tT and prop with fuel flow c_pP.

rungs.ask: From the polar, find maximum L/D.
rungs.answer: The ray from the origin tangent to the polar marks it. C_L = √(C_D0/K), parasite equals induced drag, and (L/D)max = 1/(2√(KC_D0)).
rungs.say: Maximum L/D is the tangent ray from the origin, where parasite drag equals induced drag

rungs.ask: Prop endurance. Which point do you fly?
rungs.answer: Fuel flow scales with power, so minimize P_R ∝ C_D/C_L^(3/2): C_L = √(3C_D0/K). E = (η_p/c_p)(C_L^(3/2)/C_D)√(2ρS)(W₁^(−1/2) − W₀^(−1/2)).
rungs.say: For prop endurance I minimize power, which means maximum C_L^(3/2)/C_D

rungs.ask: Prop range.
rungs.answer: R = (η_p/c_p)(L/D) ln(W₀/W₁), so fly at (L/D)max with C_L = √(C_D0/K).
rungs.say: Prop range is the Breguet equation with η_p/c_p, flown at maximum L/D

rungs.ask: Jet endurance.
rungs.answer: Fuel flow scales with thrust, so minimize drag: E = (1/c_t)(L/D) ln(W₀/W₁) at (L/D)max.
rungs.say: Jet endurance is minimum drag, maximum L/D

rungs.ask: Jet range.
rungs.answer: R = (2/c_t)√(2/(ρS))(C_L^(1/2)/C_D)(√W₀ − √W₁). Maximum C_L^(1/2)/C_D sits at C_L = √(C_D0/(3K)), where parasite drag is three times induced, and L/D = 0.866(L/D)max.
rungs.say: Jet range maximizes C_L^(1/2)/C_D, which sits at higher speed than maximum L/D

rungs.ask: Why do the jet and the prop pick different points?
rungs.answer: A jet burns fuel in proportion to thrust, so range per fuel rewards speed and moves to the √C_L/C_D point. A prop burns fuel in proportion to power, DV, which already carries the speed, so its range comes at (L/D)max and its endurance at minimum power.
rungs.say: The jet's fuel follows thrust and the prop's fuel follows power, which shifts each optimum

rungs.ask: Change the planet: fly it on Mars, electric.
rungs.answer: Battery mass stays constant, so the log term goes away: R = (e_bη/g)(L/D)(m_b/m). With g = 3.71 m/s², range per unit specific energy is 9.81/3.71 ≈ 2.6 times Earth's for the same L/D and battery fraction, while ρ ≈ 0.020 kg/m³ forces high speed and low Reynolds number lowers the achievable L/D.
rungs.say: With a battery the mass stays constant, so range is linear in L/D and in battery fraction, divided by g

rungs.ask: Now Titan.
rungs.answer: ρ ≈ 5.4 kg/m³ and g = 1.35 m/s². At fixed C_L, V scales as √(W/(ρS)), about 0.18 of the Earth speed, and power WV/(L/D) is about 2.4 percent of Earth's. Electric range per unit specific energy grows by 9.81/1.35 ≈ 7.3.
rungs.say: Titan's dense air and low gravity give slow flight at a small fraction of Earth's power

ladders.trap: Match the engine to its figure of merit: prop range at C_L = √(C_D0/K), prop endurance at C_L = √(3C_D0/K), jet endurance at (L/D)max, jet range at C_L = √(C_D0/(3K)).

ladders.title: Mission weight fractions to W₀, then make it electric
ladders.freq: Sizing loop from mission to takeoff weight is a standing aircraft design board prompt; electric aircraft appeared on a real recent board
ladders.figure: A mission profile of altitude against distance with numbered segment ends 0 to 6 (takeoff, climb, cruise, loiter, descent, landing) and the takeoff weight build-up W₀ = W_crew + W_payload + W_fuel + W_empty written beside it.

rungs.ask: Break down W₀.
rungs.answer: W₀ = W_crew + W_payload + W_fuel + W_empty.
rungs.say: Takeoff weight is crew plus payload plus fuel plus empty weight

rungs.ask: Solve it for W₀.
rungs.answer: Divide by W₀: W₀ = (W_crew + W_payload)/(1 − W_f/W₀ − W_e/W₀). The empty fraction depends on W₀, so the solution is iterative.
rungs.say: I write fuel and empty weight as fractions of W₀ and solve for W₀

rungs.ask: Where does the empty weight fraction come from?
rungs.answer: A statistical trend per aircraft class: W_e/W₀ = AW₀^C, with C slightly negative so larger aircraft carry a slightly smaller empty fraction.
rungs.say: Empty weight fraction comes from a historical trend line for the aircraft class

rungs.ask: Build the fuel fraction.
rungs.answer: Multiply segment weight fractions W_i/W_(i−1): historical values for warm-up and takeoff, climb and landing (about 0.97, 0.985, 0.995), Breguet for cruise exp(−Rc/(V(L/D))) and loiter exp(−Ec/(L/D)). Then W_f/W₀ = 1.06(1 − W₆/W₀) with 6 percent for reserve and trapped fuel.
rungs.say: I multiply the segment weight fractions and convert the final fraction into a fuel fraction with reserves

rungs.ask: Which L/D goes in cruise and loiter for a jet, and for a prop?
rungs.answer: Jet: cruise at 0.866(L/D)max, the √C_L/C_D point, and loiter at (L/D)max. Prop: cruise at (L/D)max and loiter at 0.866(L/D)max, the minimum power point.
rungs.say: The jet cruises at 0.866 of maximum L/D and loiters at maximum L/D, and the prop does the reverse

rungs.ask: Show me the loop.
rungs.answer: Guess W₀, compute W_e/W₀ from the trend, compute W₀ from the sizing equation, and repeat until the guess and the result agree. The converged value then feeds the constraint diagram for S and T.
rungs.say: Guess, evaluate the empty fraction, solve, and repeat until W₀ converges

rungs.ask: Now make it electric. What happens to the fuel fraction?
rungs.answer: Battery mass stays constant through the mission, so the Breguet log goes away. Each segment needs energy E = mgR/(η(L/D)), giving R = (e_bη/g)(L/D)(W_b/W₀) and W_b/W₀ = gR/(e_bη(L/D)), summed over segments plus a reserve and a depth of discharge margin.
rungs.say: Battery mass stays constant, so range is linear in battery fraction

rungs.ask: Solve for W₀ again.
rungs.answer: W₀ = (W_crew + W_payload)/(1 − W_b/W₀ − W_e/W₀ − W_motor/W₀). As the battery fraction grows the denominator shrinks toward zero, which gives a hard range limit. Batteries hold about 250 Wh/kg against about 12,000 Wh/kg for jet fuel.
rungs.say: The battery fraction sits in the denominator, so W₀ diverges as range approaches a hard limit

rungs.ask: What else changes in the design?
rungs.answer: Landing weight equals takeoff weight, which sizes the landing gear and puts the landing constraint at β = 1. Constant weight gives cruise at constant C_L and altitude. Motor and power electronics mass scale with peak power, so takeoff and climb size them, and thermal management adds mass.
rungs.say: Landing weight equals takeoff weight, and peak power sizes the motors

ladders.trap: Write W₀ = (W_crew + W_payload)/(1 − W_f/W₀ − W_e/W₀), iterate with W_e/W₀ = AW₀^C, and for the electric version carry a constant battery mass with R = (e_bη/g)(L/D)(W_b/W₀).
